meta.reportLabel: The euro goes back to plus 1: the November 4 flash HICP consensus is 4.0%, not the 3.8% this file assumed on Friday, and the December ECB hike is still priced above 80%.
meta.coverage: USD, EUR, GBP, JPY, AUD, NZD, CAD, CHF · 28 pairs (full G10 ex SEK/NOK) + DXY + JPYBASKET + GER40 + EU50 + XAU + XAG + XCU + USOIL
meta.regime: A weekend with no tape but two things that changed the week ahead: OPEC+ agreed in principle on Sunday to leave December output targets unchanged, so no extra barrels arrive into a Strait of Hormuz where Iran says four tankers struck mines on Friday, and the euro-area October flash HICP due Wednesday carries a 4.0% consensus against 3.8% in September. The second of those reverses this file's Friday downgrade of the euro. The energy impulse that is the stated reason for the ECB, BoE, RBA and BoC hike cycles is being renewed rather than relieved, and four of the eight currencies here have a policy decision or a national vote inside five days.
meta.nextBigEvent: Tuesday November 3 carries the RBA at 03:30Z, where all four Australian majors expect 4.85%, and the US midterms, where FXStreet analysts put a Democratic sweep near 60%; New Zealand Q3 employment lands the same evening at 21:45Z. The Bank of England follows on Thursday November 5 at 12:00Z with the Monetary Policy Report, and Friday November 6 brings US and Canadian payrolls together at 13:30Z before New Zealand votes.

dailyRead: Begin with the correction, because it is the most useful thing this file can give you today. On Friday this report cut the euro from plus 1 to zero on the German October CPI undershoot - 2.8% against 3.1% expected, with core at 2.1% and the monthly rate at minus 0.1% - and named the November 4 euro-area flash HICP at a 3.8% consensus as the test. That consensus figure was wrong. ForexFactory carries the October flash at a 4.0% forecast against 3.8% in September, and MUFG's euro-area team says a 4.0% headline is plausible; the core flash is forecast unchanged at 2.5%. The aggregate is expected to accelerate, not to follow Germany down. Alongside it, money markets still price the December 17 ECB hike above 80%, Lagarde told the October 29 press conference the Governing Council discussed a hike and agreed unanimously to hold, and MUFG expects a further 50 basis points in two steps at the December and March projection meetings. The German print is one national index inside a currency bloc whose aggregate is forecast to make a new high this week. The euro goes back to plus 1, and the leg that was supposed to have broken did not. Second, the oil side of the board was reinforced on Sunday rather than relieved. Reuters sources say OPEC+ agreed in principle at its November 1 meeting to keep December output targets unchanged, with the 2027 baselines pushed into a capacity review; the group finished unwinding the 1.65 million barrel per day voluntary cut in September and most members are still producing well below quota. That lands on a Strait of Hormuz where Iran said on Friday that four tankers struck mines, disputing the US claim that the lanes had been cleared, and where UKMTO reported a small boat attaching explosive devices to a tanker northeast of Khasab. WTI settled at 104.120 and plus 2.08%, Brent at 113.430, and WTI is plus 12.11% on the month and plus 81.33% on the year. No new supply into a mined waterway, with the US midterms on Tuesday and regional officials warning that fighting could resume around the vote, is a configuration that keeps the Canadian dollar at the top of this board and keeps USOIL long. Third, the haven question from Friday still has the same answer, and it now extends to the franc. Gold fell 3.62% to 3875.84 on a day with both an equity crash and a fresh attack in Hormuz, closing below the 3,886 level Standard Chartered flags as key support, and Kitco's technical read is that the path of least resistance remains lower; Commerzbank attributes part of the move to margin calls out of the tech selloff. Silver fell 6.22% to 48.903 and is minus 19.17% on the month, taking the gold-silver ratio to 79.26. The yen is the haven that worked, rising against all seven others on Friday, and the BoJ has now said underlying inflation has reached the 2% target for the first time since the target was set in 2013, with Takata dissenting 8-1 for a faster path and TradingEconomics forecasting 1.50% by quarter-end. The franc is the haven that did not work: USD/CHF was plus 0.07% on Friday, the SNB is the only central bank on this board with no hike in its forecast path, and a franc that cannot bid on an equity crash plus a tanker attack has told you the same thing gold did. The franc comes down to zero and sits level with the dollar. Fourth, the week's binaries. Australia goes first: the cash rate is already 4.60%, the highest since 2011, and all four majors expect 4.85% on Tuesday, but CBA calls it an insurance hike and finely balanced, Australian employment fell 39,300 in September with unemployment at 4.7% and rising, and TradingEconomics forecasts the cash rate back at 4.35% during 2027. That is a hike you own into and a path that flattens after it. Britain is the same shape with better odds: 16 of 17 houses surveyed expect 4.00% on Thursday and Polymarket prices the 25 basis point increase at 77%, with ForexFactory carrying a 7-0-2 vote forecast against September's 6-3 hold and Rabobank expecting Dhingra and Taylor to dissent - but TradingEconomics has the Bank Rate flat at 4.00% through 2027, so the Monetary Policy Report is where a 77%-priced hike can still be sold. Note that this file carried 94% on Friday; the verifiable market number is 77%, and the direction is unchanged while the certainty is lower. New Zealand is the one that moves down. The RBNZ declined on October 28 a hike the market had near 90%, on a 4-3 vote; the kiwi is the week's worst major at minus 1.19%; Q3 employment arrives Tuesday at 21:45Z with unemployment forecast at 5.5% from 5.6%; and the general election on Saturday November 7 has no clear outcome in the polls, with RNZ-Reid Research putting Labour at 30.8% against National at 25.9% while 1News-Verian has National 29% and Labour 27%, and The Opportunity Party polling anywhere from 5% to 9.5% as the coalition wildcard. The kiwi goes to minus 1 and gives this board the bottom it has been missing. Be clear about which leg that is: it is the election binary and the credibility discount, not the rate path, because TradingEconomics still forecasts 3.00% by quarter-end and Breman said rates may end higher than the September meeting implied. Finally the dollar, which stays at zero and is the least interesting currency on the board this week precisely because it has the most events. The December 9 hike is priced between 71% and 83% depending on the source and the hour, the October hold was 10-2 with Cook and Hammack preferring a quarter point, Q3 GDP printed 3.4% and core PCE 3.1%, and Chair Warsh has reiterated his opposition to forward guidance and announced fewer rate-setting meetings from 2027. Against that, Tuesday's midterms are a genuine two-sided event - FXStreet puts a Democratic sweep near 60%, a House-only win near 30% and a Republican hold near 10%, and Convera argues the Republican sweep is the larger tail for yields and the dollar - and Friday's payrolls are forecast at 63,000 after 29,000. DXY closed at 101.879, minus 0.22% on the month. The cleanest expressions of all of this are the three-point gaps: GBP/NZD and AUD/NZD long, NZD/CAD short. The cleanest single-catalyst trade is EUR/USD long into Wednesday's 10:00Z flash HICP, small, because it is a one-point gap and the dollar leg votes the day before.

today.headline: Restored to plus 1 from zero within a day, on a specific fact: the November 4 flash HICP consensus is 4.0% against 3.8% in September, not the 3.8% this file used on Friday to justify the downgrade.
today.read: The distinction that matters is between one national index and the aggregate. German October CPI did undershoot at 2.8% with core at 2.1%, and German Q3 GDP slowed to 0.2% q/q - but ForexFactory and MUFG both carry the euro-area flash at 4.0%, core flat at 2.5%, and money markets still price December 17 above 80%. TradingEconomics is the clincher: its refi forecast rises from 2.90% this quarter to 3.15% during 2027, the only currency here whose 2027 path sits above its near-term path. The standing risk is no longer the data; it is governance, with Lagarde leaving on February 7 and Knot and de Cos named as leading contenders while Schnabel and Lane also turn over. Wednesday at 10:00Z settles the data leg.

today.headline: Cut to minus 1 and to the bottom of the board, with a general election on Saturday November 7 that the polls cannot call and Q3 employment on Tuesday at 21:45Z.
today.read: Say plainly which leg this is. It is not the rate path: the RBNZ said further tightening would likely be needed, Breman said rates may end higher than September implied, and TradingEconomics still forecasts 3.00% by December 9. It is the combination of a 4-3 refusal to deliver a hike the market had near 90%, a kiwi that is the week's worst major at minus 1.19%, and a binary national vote inside the horizon with RNZ-Reid Research at Labour 30.8% to National 25.9% and 1News-Verian at National 29% to Labour 27%, under a proportional system where The Opportunity Party at 5% to 9.5% decides the coalition. A 5.5% unemployment print on Tuesday is the first thing that would start repairing this.

today.headline: Cut to zero and level with the dollar: the franc was plus 0.07% against it on a day with a 2.86% Nasdaq fall and four tankers mined, which is a haven that did not bid.
today.read: This is the same test gold failed and the yen passed, applied to the franc. Underneath the price action the structure is thin: the SNB is the only central bank here with no hike anywhere in its forecast path, TradingEconomics carries 0.00% this quarter and only 0.75% during 2027, CPI is 1.0% with core at 0.5%, and the Bank repeated in September that it stands ready to intervene in FX - a standing bid against franc strength. Swiss CPI lands Tuesday at 07:30Z with a 0.0% m/m forecast and Schlegel speaks Thursday at 12:40Z. A genuine escalation in Hormuz is what would put the franc back to plus 1.

today.headline: Stays at the top of the board and the reason was reinforced on Sunday: OPEC+ agreed in principle to leave December output targets unchanged with WTI at 104.120 and Hormuz mined.
today.read: Canada is the only currency here with a delivered hike, a forecast follow-up and a rising export price at the same time. The October 28 move to 2.50% was the first in three years, the statement kept the door open with the line about a possible need to increase further, TradingEconomics forecasts 2.75% by quarter-end, and the Bank lifted its 2027 CPI projection to 3% from 2%. The weak leg is domestic labour: employment fell 68,300 in September and Friday's print is forecast at plus 14,500 with unemployment at 6.5%. Macklem speaks twice this week, Tuesday 16:00Z and Thursday 15:30Z. An accepted Iran deal that reopens the Strait is still the single clean invalidation.

today.headline: Holds plus 2 into Thursday's decision, but the honest market number is 77% on Polymarket rather than the 94% this file carried on Friday.
today.read: The direction is not in doubt - sixteen of seventeen houses expect 4.00% - but the certainty is lower than stated and that changes how much of the move is left. The tradeable content is in the vote and the Report: ForexFactory forecasts 7-0-2 against September's 6-3 hold, Rabobank expects Dhingra and Taylor to dissent, and TradingEconomics then has Bank Rate flat at 4.00% through 2027. A Report that caps the path at 4.00% sells a hike that is three-quarters priced. Supporting data is firm: CPI 3.5% with core 2.8%, unemployment down to 4.7%, employment plus 102,000 and wage growth 3.7%. Bailey speaks at 12:30Z and Pill on Friday.

today.headline: Holds plus 2 with the highest policy rate on the board at 4.60% and a 4.85% consensus on Tuesday, but the forward turns balanced rather than hawkish.
today.read: Three things sit under Tuesday. The case for the hike is September CPI at 4.3% with core 3.6%, Hauser calling the inflation outlook materially worse, and all four majors on board. The case for caution is that CBA, which changed its call, describes it as an insurance hike and finely balanced, that employment fell 39,300 in September with unemployment at 4.7% and rising, and that GDP has slowed to 2.1% y/y from 2.5%. The case for fading what comes after is TradingEconomics, which forecasts 4.85% this quarter and then 4.35% during 2027 - this is a terminal hike, not the middle of a cycle. The press conference at 04:30Z is where that distinction gets priced.

today.headline: Stays plus 1 but the forward is now firmly hawkish: the BoJ said underlying inflation has reached 2% for the first time since the target was set in 2013, and Takata dissented 8-1 for a faster path.
today.read: The backward verdict stays mixed because the carry has kept winning - the yen is only minus 0.34% on the month and USD/JPY is 157.561 - but the forward evidence has accumulated to the point where it should be traded. The Bank raised its FY2027 inflation forecast to 2.6% from 2.4% and its FY2026 growth forecast to 0.7%, TradingEconomics forecasts 1.50% by quarter-end, and Commerzbank calls December almost fully priced. Friday added the market evidence: the yen rose against all seven other currencies here while gold fell 3.62%, which is the haven bid rotating. Ueda speaks Friday at 16:00Z and has stayed deliberately vague on timing. Above 158 the Ministry of Finance becomes the other participant.

today.headline: Unchanged at zero with the most events and the least direction: December pricing spans 71% to 83%, the midterms are Tuesday and payrolls are Friday.
today.read: The data since the October 28 hold has supported the two dissenters rather than the majority - Q3 GDP 3.4%, core PCE 3.1%, core CPI up to 2.6% - but the pricing has not consolidated, which is what keeps this at zero rather than plus 1. Tuesday is the genuine two-sided risk: FXStreet analysts put a Democratic sweep near 60%, a House-only win near 30% and a Republican hold near 10%, and Convera argues the Republican tail is the one that would move yields and the dollar most. Friday's payrolls are forecast at 63,000 after 29,000 with unemployment at 4.2% and average hourly earnings at 0.3%. DXY is 101.879 and minus 0.22% on the month.

USD.note: Held at 4.00% upper bound on October 28 by a 10-2 vote, with Cook and Hammack preferring a quarter point. TradingEconomics forecasts 4.25% by quarter-end and holds that level through 2027 before 4.00% in 2028. Market pricing for December ran between 71% and 83% across the week depending on source and hour, which is a wide band for a decision five weeks out.

EUR.when: December 17, confirmed on the ECB's own calendar as the final 2026 meeting
EUR.note: Deposit facility held at 2.50% on October 29 with the refi rate at 2.65%, and Lagarde said the Council discussed a hike and agreed unanimously to hold. Money markets price December above 80%. TradingEconomics forecasts the refi rate at 2.90% this quarter and 3.15% during 2027, which maps to a 2.75% deposit rate by year-end and 3.00% next year - the only path on this board whose 2027 level sits above its current-quarter level.

GBP.when: November 5 at 12:00Z, with the Monetary Policy Report
GBP.note: Bank Rate 3.75% after a 6-3 hold on September 16. Sixteen of seventeen houses surveyed expect 4.00% and Polymarket prices the increase at 77%; ForexFactory carries a 7-0-2 vote forecast and Rabobank expects Dhingra and Taylor to dissent. TradingEconomics then has the rate flat at 4.00% through 2027, so the Report is where the path, not the decision, is decided.

JPY.when: December 18, with Ueda still declining to date it
JPY.note: Held at 1.25% on October 30 by 8-1, Takata dissenting for a faster path to neutral. The Bank said underlying inflation has aligned with the 2% target for the first time since 2013, raised its FY2027 inflation forecast to 2.6% from 2.4% and its FY2026 growth forecast to 0.7%. TradingEconomics forecasts 1.50% by quarter-end; Commerzbank calls December almost fully priced. Ueda speaks November 6 at 16:00Z.

AUD.when: November 3 at 03:30Z, with the Statement on Monetary Policy
AUD.note: Cash rate 4.60% after a unanimous September 29 hike, the fourth of the year and the highest since 2011. All four majors expect 4.85%; TradingEconomics forecasts the same. CBA, which had expected a hold, calls it an insurance hike and finely balanced, and Deputy Governor Hauser said the inflation outlook is materially worse. TradingEconomics then has 4.35% during 2027 - the path flattens and turns down after Tuesday.

NZD.when: December 9, with a full Monetary Policy Statement
NZD.note: Held at 2.75% on October 28 against a 3.00% forecast and pricing near 90%, on a 4-3 vote. The Committee said further tightening would likely be needed and Breman said rates may end higher than September implied; TradingEconomics forecasts 3.00% by quarter-end. The path is intact - what is damaged is the credibility of the timing, and the November 7 election sits in front of it.

CAD.note: Hiked 25 basis points to 2.50% on October 28, the first increase in three years, with the statement saying there could be a need to increase further while cautious is necessary. The Bank now sees CPI averaging 3% in 2027, a full point above its July projection. TradingEconomics forecasts 2.75% by quarter-end and holds that through 2027, so a second hike in December is its base case.

CHF.note: Policy rate at 0% since mid-2025 and held again on September 24. The SNB expects inflation to rise further in the fourth quarter before easing, forecasts 0.7% average inflation in 2026 and 0.8% in 2027 and 2028, and repeated that it remains willing to intervene in FX as necessary. TradingEconomics forecasts 0.00% this quarter and only 0.75% during 2027. Chairman Schlegel speaks November 5 at 12:40Z.

symbols.risk: Both legs print payrolls at the same minute on Friday at 13:30Z - US at a 63,000 forecast, Canada at plus 14,500 after minus 68,300 - which is the one moment this trade is genuinely two-sided. The structural exit is an accepted Iran deal that reopens the Strait. Macklem speaks Tuesday 16:00Z and Thursday 15:30Z.

symbols.why: A two-point gap at 0.70324 and plus 1.47% on the month, into an RBA decision on Tuesday at 03:30Z where all four Australian majors and TradingEconomics expect 4.85% from the highest policy rate on this board.
symbols.risk: The hike is owned, so the move is in the Statement on Monetary Policy and the 04:30Z press conference. CBA calls it an insurance hike and finely balanced; employment fell 39,300 in September and TradingEconomics has the cash rate back at 4.35% during 2027, so a terminal-sounding statement fades this fast. The dollar leg then votes the same day.

symbols.why: Turns SHORT at 0.56300 on the kiwi's cut to minus 1: the week's worst major at minus 1.19%, a 4-3 refusal to deliver a hike priced near 90%, and a general election on Saturday that the polls cannot call.
symbols.risk: Only a one-point gap, and the dollar is the least reliable short leg this week with midterms on Tuesday and payrolls on Friday. Prefer the kiwi crosses against CAD or AUD for a cleaner expression. Q3 employment on Tuesday at 21:45Z, forecast at 5.5% unemployment from 5.6%, is the first thing that would repair the kiwi leg.

symbols.why: A zero-point gap at 0.82496 now that the franc has come down to zero alongside the dollar - both are the currencies on this board with the least tightening ahead of them, and the pair was plus 0.07% on Friday.
symbols.risk: Trade the levels with the month's 0.73% decline as the trend. The asymmetry is in the tails rather than the middle: a Hormuz closure bids the franc and a hawkish December Fed bids the dollar, and the SNB's standing willingness to intervene sits under the pair. Swiss CPI Tuesday 07:30Z and Schlegel Thursday 12:40Z.

symbols.why: Turns from SHORT to RANGE at about 175.81 because both legs were upgraded at once - the euro back to plus 1 on the 4.0% HICP consensus, and the yen carrying the board's most hawkish forward after the BoJ hit its 2% target.
symbols.risk: This is now a zero-point gap between two currencies that both have a December hike as the base case - the ECB on the 17th above 80% priced, the BoJ on the 18th almost fully priced - which is the definition of a range. Trade levels. Whichever flash print lands further from consensus on Wednesday breaks the tie.

symbols.why: Downgraded from MEDIUM to LOW-MED at about 1.5867: the gap has narrowed to one point because the euro was restored to plus 1, even though the Australian hike on Tuesday remains the nearer and more certain catalyst.
symbols.risk: Two hawkish currencies two days apart makes this a timing trade. The RBA goes first on Tuesday and the euro-area print lands Wednesday, so an insurance-sounding RBA followed by a 4.0% HICP flips this long inside 36 hours. TradingEconomics has the Australian path turning down in 2027 and the euro path turning up - over the full horizon that argues for closing this out rather than adding.

symbols.why: Turns from RANGE to LONG at about 1.9819 on a two-point gap opened from both ends at once: the euro restored to plus 1 on the 4.0% HICP consensus and the kiwi cut to minus 1 on the November 7 election binary.
symbols.risk: Both legs are event-driven inside the week, so this carries two dated risks rather than one. A 3-handle euro-area flash on Wednesday removes the euro leg; a 5.5% New Zealand unemployment print on Tuesday plus a decisive election result removes the kiwi leg. Prefer GBP/NZD or AUD/NZD if you want the kiwi short without the euro event.

symbols.why: Conviction cut from HIGH to LOW-MED at about 0.8332: the gap closed from two points to one when the euro was restored, and sterling's own catalyst is now priced at 77% rather than the 94% this file carried on Friday.
symbols.risk: The two central banks are moving in the same direction within six weeks of each other, so this is a path trade rather than a level trade. TradingEconomics has Bank Rate flat at 4.00% through 2027 while the ECB refi path rises to 3.15% - if Thursday's Monetary Policy Report confirms a terminal 4.00% and Wednesday's flash prints 4.0%, this turns long. Hold it small into Thursday.

symbols.why: Conviction cut from HIGH to LOW-MED at about 1.5592 on the euro's restoration to plus 1, which closes the gap to a single point against a Canadian dollar still carrying oil at 104.120 and a December hike as TradingEconomics base case.
symbols.risk: Canada's leg is the sturdier of the two but it is also the one with the clearer exit - an accepted Iran deal reopens the Strait and takes the oil premium out at once. The euro leg resolves Wednesday at 10:00Z. With both central banks expected to hike in December this is a one-point gap between two hawks, so trade it small and watch Friday's twin payrolls.

symbols.why: Turns from SHORT to LONG at about 0.9205 after both legs moved in opposite directions on the same day: the euro restored to plus 1 on the HICP consensus, the franc cut to zero as the haven that would not bid on Friday's equity crash.
symbols.risk: The SNB's stated readiness to intervene in FX works in this trade's favour rather than against it, but 0.92 is an area where official interest cuts both ways and liquidity is thin. Keep it small. A genuine Hormuz closure bids the franc faster than the euro and reverses this; Wednesday's flash HICP and Schlegel on Thursday are the two scheduled tests.

symbols.why: Holds LONG at about 211.00 on a one-point gap, with sterling's November 5 hike arriving six weeks before the BoJ's expected December 18 move, so the near-term carry still favours the pound.
symbols.risk: This is the trade that most depends on the yen staying asleep, and Friday was the first evidence in weeks that it will not - the yen rose against all seven others while gold fell. The BoJ has now hit its 2% target and TradingEconomics forecasts 1.50% by quarter-end. A capped Monetary Policy Report on Thursday plus a hawkish Ueda on Friday turns this short quickly at a level this high.

symbols.why: A zero-point gap at about 1.9043 between the two currencies with the nearest decisions - the RBA on Tuesday at a 4.85% consensus and the Bank of England on Thursday at 4.00% - both of which look terminal on TradingEconomics 2027 forecasts.
symbols.risk: Two decisions in three days makes this the week's cleanest event range rather than a directional trade. Trade the levels and let the two statements settle it: the one that sounds more open-ended wins. TradingEconomics has Australia at 4.35% during 2027 against the UK flat at 4.00%, which slightly favours sterling over the full horizon.

symbols.why: The widest gap on the board at three points, at about 2.3786: sterling at plus 2 into Thursday's hike against a kiwi cut to minus 1 on a general election the polls cannot call and a central bank that just refused a hike priced near 90%.
symbols.risk: Both legs are dated inside the week, which is the risk and the reason. A Monetary Policy Report that caps the path at 4.00% takes the sterling leg down; a 5.5% unemployment print on Tuesday plus a decisive November 7 result repairs the kiwi. Be out or reduced before Saturday's vote, because an election gap is not a 4H risk you can manage.

symbols.why: A zero-point gap at about 1.8713 between the board's two joint-strongest currencies, with sterling hiking Thursday and Canada carrying oil at 104.120 plus a December hike as TradingEconomics base case.
symbols.risk: Both print labour data on Friday - the UK does not, but Canada does at 13:30Z alongside the US - so the Canadian leg has the later catalyst. Trade the levels into Thursday, then let the Monetary Policy Report and the Canadian jobs number resolve it. An Iran deal weakens the Canadian leg and turns this long.

symbols.why: Upgraded to a two-point gap at about 1.1047 after the franc was cut to zero: sterling has a hike on Thursday with sixteen of seventeen houses behind it, while the SNB is the only central bank here with no hike anywhere in its forecast path.
symbols.risk: The franc leg is a slow structural short and the sterling leg is a fast event, which is a mismatch of horizons. The risk is a Hormuz escalation that bids the franc before Thursday, or a Monetary Policy Report that caps the sterling path. Schlegel speaks Thursday at 12:40Z, forty minutes after the Bank of England decision.

symbols.why: Holds a small LONG at about 110.80 on a one-point gap, with the RBA hiking Tuesday to a 4.85% consensus six weeks ahead of the BoJ's expected December 18 move, so the carry differential still widens first.
symbols.risk: The classic risk-on carry pair into a week when the AI unwind is the live equity story - the Nasdaq fell 2.86% on Friday and is down 5.3% on the month. If that extends, this pair loses on both legs at once. TradingEconomics has Australia easing to 4.35% during 2027 while Japan tightens, which makes this a trade with a short shelf life.

symbols.why: A three-point gap at about 1.2491 with both catalysts on the same day: the RBA hikes Tuesday at 03:30Z to a 4.85% consensus, and New Zealand Q3 employment lands eighteen hours later at 21:45Z with the election five days after that.
symbols.risk: The cleanest antipodean divergence available, and the one place where the kiwi short does not depend on the dollar. A hold or an insurance-sounding RBA statement on Tuesday morning removes half the trade before the New Zealand data even prints. Reduce before Saturday's vote - a coalition result that lands cleanly can retrace a week of this in one gap.

symbols.why: A zero-point gap at about 0.9827 between two commodity currencies both at plus 2, one hiking Tuesday and the other carrying WTI at 104.120 after OPEC+ agreed in principle on Sunday to leave December output unchanged.
symbols.risk: The two legs respond to the same Middle East premium in opposite ways - higher oil is a direct Canadian terms-of-trade gain and an Australian inflation problem that forces more RBA tightening - which is exactly why this stays a range. Copper at 6.4585 and minus 1.86% is the Australian side's own read. Canadian jobs Friday 13:30Z.

symbols.why: Upgraded to a two-point gap at about 0.5801 after the franc fell to zero: the highest policy rate on this board hiking again on Tuesday against a 0% rate that TradingEconomics forecasts stays at 0.00% this quarter.
symbols.risk: The widest rate differential available here, which also makes it the most exposed to a risk-off franc bid - the position that pays most when nothing happens loses most when something does. A Hormuz escalation hits this twice, bidding the franc while Australian equities follow Wall Street. Tuesday's RBA statement is the near catalyst.

symbols.why: Upgraded from LOW-MED on a now two-point gap at about 88.71: the kiwi cut to minus 1 on the November 7 election and the RBNZ's 4-3 refusal, against a yen that rose against all seven others on Friday and now has a December hike as the BoJ base case.
symbols.risk: Both legs pull the same way, which is rare, but the yen leg has been the perennial disappointment - the carry has won all month with the yen at minus 0.34%. The Ministry of Finance intervening near 160 would help this trade; a sharp recovery in risk appetite hurts both legs at once. Ueda speaks Friday at 16:00Z.

symbols.why: A three-point gap at about 0.7867, the mirror of GBP/NZD: the kiwi at minus 1 on an election binary and a credibility discount, against the only currency here with a delivered hike, a forecast follow-up and a rising export price.
symbols.risk: Both legs print labour data this week - New Zealand on Tuesday at 21:45Z with unemployment forecast at 5.5%, Canada on Friday at 13:30Z with employment forecast at plus 14,500 after minus 68,300 - so there are two scheduled reversals available. An accepted Iran deal would hit the Canadian leg hard. Reduce before Saturday's New Zealand vote.

symbols.why: Holds SHORT at about 0.4645 but on a narrowed one-point gap, because the franc was cut to zero on the same day the kiwi went to minus 1 - both legs weakened, and only the margin between them survives.
symbols.risk: Two weak currencies make a weak trade. The kiwi leg is the one with the dated catalysts - employment Tuesday, election Saturday - while the franc leg is structurally soft but would bid instantly on a Hormuz closure. Prefer NZD/CAD or AUD/NZD for the same kiwi short with a stronger other leg.

symbols.why: Conviction cut from MEDIUM at about 112.76: the gap is now one point rather than two because the yen's forward has turned firmly hawkish, even though the Canadian leg was reinforced by Sunday's OPEC+ decision to hold December output.
symbols.risk: This is long oil and short the one haven that is currently working, which is a coherent trade only while the Middle East premium rises without a risk-off wave attached. Friday brought both at once and the yen won. Canadian jobs Friday 13:30Z and Ueda the same day at 16:00Z sit on the same session.

symbols.why: Upgraded to a two-point gap at about 0.5904 after the franc fell to zero: Canada carries a delivered hike, a December follow-up as TradingEconomics base case and WTI at 104.120, against a 0% rate with no hike in its path.
symbols.risk: Both legs key off the same Middle East headline in opposite directions, so this is effectively a leveraged long on the Hormuz premium. An accepted Iran deal hits it twice - oil falls and the franc holds. Qatari mediators are in Tehran and Trump says the conflict ends very soon, so size for a headline gap.

symbols.why: Turns from RANGE to SHORT at about 190.99 on a one-point gap opened by the franc's downgrade to zero: Friday was a direct comparison of the two havens on the same day and the yen won against all seven others while the franc was flat.
symbols.risk: Both are havens, so a genuine escalation bids them together and the trade goes nowhere - this works on the relative quality of the two bids, not on the regime. The yen leg has the better fundamental story with the BoJ at its 2% target and December almost fully priced. Schlegel Thursday 12:40Z, Ueda Friday 16:00Z.

symbols.why: A small SHORT at 101.879 and minus 0.22% on the month: every weighted component outranks the dollar at zero - the euro back to plus 1 at 57.6%, the yen plus 1 at 13.6%, sterling plus 2 at 11.9% and the Canadian dollar plus 2 at 9.1%.
symbols.risk: The index is dominated by the euro leg, so Wednesday's 10:00Z flash HICP is effectively this trade's catalyst, and Tuesday's midterms are the dollar-side event that comes first. Convera's view that a Republican sweep is the larger tail for yields and the dollar is the main reversal case. Payrolls Friday at a 63,000 forecast.

symbols.why: Stays RANGE because the yen's verdict stays MIXED: the forward is the most hawkish on the board after the BoJ hit its 2% target, but spot has not confirmed it with the yen only minus 0.34% on the month.
symbols.risk: This is the opposite ticket to every XXX/JPY pair, so it is the single instrument that expresses the whole yen view - which is exactly why it should wait for the verdict to turn rather than anticipate it. A December hike confirmed in Ueda's Friday remarks, or an intervention near 160, turns this long. Trade the levels until then.

symbols.why: Turns from RANGE to a small SHORT at 25,818 after Friday's 0.85% fall snapped a four-day run, with Brent rising to 113.430 rather than falling and TradingEconomics carrying a Q4 forecast of 25,353, about 1.8% below spot.
symbols.risk: The dominant leg is the AI capex unwind rather than rates - Infineon, Siemens Energy and Hochtief lost between 3% and 7.1% on Friday - and the index is still plus 3.52% on the month, so this is fading strength, not chasing weakness. The offsetting tailwind is real: German October CPI at 2.8% with core 2.1% is the best inflation print in the bloc.

symbols.why: Holds SHORT at 6,131.31 on its own evidence rather than the DAX's: it is minus 0.71% on the month while GER40 is plus 3.52%, a four-point divergence, and TradingEconomics carries a Q4 forecast of 6,023, about 1.8% below spot.
symbols.risk: The banks leg is the one to watch because it argues the other way - a December ECB hike now priced above 80% and a refi path rising to 3.15% in 2027 helps the index's heaviest sector. But Friday showed banks underperforming anyway, with NatWest down 9% and Credit Agricole down more than 2%, while tech led the fall with ASML down around 6%. Add the French political overhang and the Lagarde succession, and the tech plus politics legs are dominating the rates leg.

symbols.why: Stays SHORT at 3875.84 after Friday's 3.62% fall closed it below the 3,886 level Standard Chartered flags as key support, on a day that carried both a 2.86% Nasdaq decline and four mined tankers and still could not bid it.
symbols.risk: The evidence is the failure, not the level. Kitco reads the path of least resistance as lower and Commerzbank attributes part of the move to margin calls out of the tech selloff, but Commerzbank also expects a recovery and notes central bank buying tends to pick up below 4,000. A dovish turn in December Fed pricing or a Hormuz closure are the two clean reversals; gold is minus 7.23% on the month and minus 10.28% on the year.

symbols.why: Stays SHORT at 48.903 after a 6.22% fall took silver below 50 for the first time in about eleven months, with the industrial leg now compounding the precious one as the AI capex story turns down.
symbols.risk: Silver is minus 19.17% on the month and minus 31.37% on the year against gold's minus 10.28%, which has taken the ratio to 79.26 from 76.8 - a stretched move that mean-reverts violently. HSBC cut its 2027 average forecast to 64 from 71 on weaker industrial and jewellery demand, and some analysts see the mid-40s if selling continues. Copper at minus 1.86% confirms the industrial read for now.

symbols.why: Stays RANGE at 6.4585 USD/lb and minus 1.86% on Friday, with a genuinely two-sided physical picture: LME warehouse stocks fell to 231,275 tonnes on October 9 from 324,850 at end-June, while COMEX holds roughly 718,200 tonnes on tariff front-running.
symbols.risk: Tight exchange stocks outside the US against a softening demand read - Chinese copper demand was flat year on year as nearly 10% export-related growth offset a 5% domestic decline, and LME Week sentiment turned more cautious on tariff uncertainty. Copper is still plus 13.67% on the year and plus 26.94% year on year, which is the trend this range sits inside. Tie it to the Australian dollar at plus 2.

symbols.why: Stays LONG at 104.120 and plus 2.08%, with the supply leg reinforced on Sunday: Reuters sources say OPEC+ agreed in principle to leave December output targets unchanged, so no new barrels arrive while Iran says four tankers struck mines in Hormuz on Friday.
symbols.risk: This remains a binary, not a trend. Trump says the conflict will end very soon, Vice President Vance is seeking to reopen talks and Qatari mediators are in Tehran - an accepted deal reopens the Strait and takes out a premium that has carried WTI plus 12.11% on the month and plus 81.33% on the year. The other direction is Tuesday's midterms, around which regional officials warn fighting could resume. Keep this consistent with the Canadian dollar at plus 2.

inflation.note: Sep HICP; Oct flash Nov 4 fc 4.0%

rates.note: OCR, held Oct 28 on a 4-3 vote

catalysts.event: Australia: CPI m/m, CPI y/y and Trimmed Mean CPI m/m (ABS red folder)
catalysts.note: Released. Headline CPI printed above forecast at 4.3% y/y against 4.2% expected, with TradingEconomics carrying core at 3.6% and the trimmed mean at 3.7%. This is the print that moved all four Australian majors onto a November 3 hike and made CBA switch its call.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: RBNZ Official Cash Rate decision and Rate Statement (red folder)
catalysts.note: Released. Held at 2.75% against a 3.00% forecast and pricing near 90%, on a 4-3 vote. Four days on, the kiwi is the week's worst major at minus 1.19% and this file now scores that as a credibility discount rather than an economic verdict.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: RBNZ press conference with Governor Breman (red folder)
catalysts.note: Held. Breman said further increases are likely at coming meetings and that rates may end higher than the September meeting implied. TradingEconomics still forecasts a 3.00% OCR by quarter-end, which is why the kiwi downgrade is explicitly not a rate-path call.

catalysts.event: United Kingdom: Annual Budget Release (HM Treasury red folder)
catalysts.note: Delivered, and the tail did not happen - ten-year gilt yields fell on the day. That cleared the main obstacle in front of the November 5 hike and is a large part of why sterling still holds plus 2.

catalysts.event: Canada: BoC Overnight Rate, Rate Statement and Monetary Policy Report (red folder)
catalysts.note: Released. Hiked 25 basis points to 2.50%, the first increase in three years, with the statement saying there could be a need to increase the policy rate further. The Bank lifted its 2027 CPI projection to 3%, a full point above July, and now sees growth of 1% in 2026 and 2% in 2027 and 2028.

catalysts.event: United States: FOMC statement and federal funds rate (red folder)
catalysts.note: Released. Held at 3.75%-4.00% on a 10-2 vote, with Cook and Hammack preferring a quarter-point hike. The statement said activity is expanding at a strong pace and inflation remains elevated. Chair Warsh also announced the Fed will reduce the number of meetings at which members vote on rates from 2027.

catalysts.event: Euro area: ECB main refinancing rate, deposit facility rate and Lagarde press conference (red folder)
catalysts.note: Held, refi at 2.65% and the deposit facility at 2.50%. Lagarde confirmed the Council discussed a hike and agreed unanimously to hold, and warned elevated energy prices could fuel inflation while weighing on activity. She separately announced she will leave the ECB early, on February 7 2027.

catalysts.event: Japan: BoJ policy rate, Outlook Report and Ueda press conference (red folder)
catalysts.note: Released. Held at 1.25% by 8-1 with Takata dissenting for a faster path to neutral. The Bank said underlying CPI inflation had aligned with the 2% target for the first time since the target was set in 2013, raised its FY2027 inflation forecast to 2.6% from 2.4% and lifted FY2026 growth to 0.7%.

catalysts.event: Germany: Preliminary October CPI (Destatis red folder)
catalysts.note: Released. Headline fell to 2.8% y/y from 3.3% against about 3.1% expected, with core at 2.1% from 2.4% and the harmonised monthly rate at minus 0.1%. This file cut the euro on it and has now reversed that: the euro-area aggregate is forecast to accelerate to 4.0% on Wednesday.

catalysts.event: OPEC+ ministerial meeting on December quotas
catalysts.note: Reuters sources say the group agreed in principle to leave December output targets unchanged, with 2027 baselines deferred to a fourth-quarter capacity review. No official communique had been published at the time of writing, so treat it as sourced rather than confirmed. Most members are producing well below quota.

catalysts.event: United States: ISM Manufacturing PMI
catalysts.note: Forecast 54.7 after 54.5. The prices-paid component at a 77.2 forecast is the one that matters for the December hike debate, given core PCE at 3.1%.

catalysts.event: Australia: RBA Cash Rate, Rate Statement and Statement on Monetary Policy (red folder)
catalysts.note: Forecast 4.85% from 4.60%. All four Australian majors expect the hike and TradingEconomics forecasts the same; CBA calls it an insurance hike and finely balanced. The tradeable content is whether the statement signals a terminal rate, since TradingEconomics has the cash rate back at 4.35% during 2027.

catalysts.event: Australia: RBA press conference (red folder)
catalysts.note: One hour after the decision. Deputy Governor Hauser has already said the inflation outlook is materially worse than forecast; the question is whether the Board frames Tuesday as insurance against embedded inflation or as the start of a further leg.

catalysts.event: Switzerland: CPI m/m
catalysts.note: Forecast 0.0% m/m, unchanged. Headline is 1.0% y/y with core at 0.5%; the SNB expects inflation to rise further in the fourth quarter before easing, and forecasts a 0.7% average for 2026.

catalysts.event: United States: Congressional midterm elections (red folder)
catalysts.note: FXStreet analysts put a Democratic sweep near 60%, a House-only win near 30% and a Republican hold near 10%. Convera argues the Republican sweep is the larger tail for Treasury yields and the dollar. Regional officials also warn Middle East fighting could resume around the vote.

catalysts.event: Canada: BoC Governor Macklem speaks
catalysts.note: First remarks since the October 28 hike. Watch for how firmly he defends the line about a possible need to increase the policy rate further, which is what TradingEconomics 2.75% quarter-end forecast rests on.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: Q3 Employment Change and Unemployment Rate (red folder)
catalysts.note: Forecast unemployment 5.5% from 5.6% and employment plus 0.4% q/q from plus 0.5%. This is the first scheduled chance to repair the kiwi downgrade, and it lands four days before the general election.

catalysts.event: Euro area: October flash HICP and core flash estimate
catalysts.note: The single most important scheduled number for this board. Headline forecast 4.0% y/y from 3.8%, core forecast unchanged at 2.5%; MUFG calls a 4.0% headline plausible. A 3-handle aggregate takes the euro straight back to zero and reverses EUR/USD, EUR/NZD and EUR/CHF.

catalysts.event: United States: ISM Services PMI
catalysts.note: Forecast 54.9, unchanged. The first US data point after the midterms and a check on the strong-pace language in the October FOMC statement.

catalysts.event: United Kingdom: Official Bank Rate, Monetary Policy Summary, MPC vote and Monetary Policy Report (red folder)
catalysts.note: Forecast 4.00% from 3.75%, with a 7-0-2 vote forecast against September's 6-3 hold. Sixteen of seventeen houses expect the hike and Polymarket prices it at 77%. Rabobank expects Dhingra and Taylor to dissent. TradingEconomics then has Bank Rate flat at 4.00% through 2027, so the Report decides the path.

catalysts.event: United Kingdom: BoE Governor Bailey speaks (red folder)
catalysts.note: The press conference half of the decision. Whether Bailey frames 4.00% as terminal or as a step is what separates a sterling extension from selling a three-quarters-priced hike.

catalysts.event: Switzerland: SNB Chairman Schlegel speaks
catalysts.note: Forty minutes after the Bank of England. The franc was cut to zero in this report on its failure to bid on Friday, and the standing question is how willing the SNB is to act on its stated readiness to intervene in FX.

catalysts.event: Canada: BoC Governor Macklem speaks
catalysts.note: His second appearance of the week, the day before Canadian payrolls. September employment fell 68,300, which is the clearest weak spot in an otherwise complete Canadian case.

catalysts.event: Euro area: ECB President Lagarde speaks
catalysts.note: Her first scheduled remarks after confirming she will leave on February 7 2027. Reuters names Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernandez de Cos as leading contenders, with Schnabel and Lane also due to turn over.

catalysts.event: United States: Non-Farm Employment Change, Unemployment Rate and Average Hourly Earnings (red folder)
catalysts.note: Forecast plus 63,000 after 29,000, unemployment 4.2% unchanged and average hourly earnings 0.3% m/m after 0.1%. The data resolution for a December hike that has been pricing anywhere between 71% and 83%.

catalysts.event: Canada: Employment Change and Unemployment Rate (red folder)
catalysts.note: Forecast plus 14,500 after minus 68,300, with unemployment at 6.5% unchanged. Lands at the same minute as the US print, which makes USD/CAD the one pair with genuine two-sided risk in that second.

catalysts.event: Japan: BoJ Governor Ueda speaks (red folder)
catalysts.note: Ueda stayed deliberately vague on timing at the October 30 press conference, saying the Bank will keep raising the rate while flagging FX, AI and Middle East risks. TradingEconomics forecasts 1.50% by quarter-end and Commerzbank calls December 18 almost fully priced.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: General election (red folder)
catalysts.note: Polls open Saturday November 7 local time. No clear outcome: RNZ-Reid Research has Labour 30.8% to National 25.9%, 1News-Verian has National 29% to Labour 27%, and under the mixed member proportional system The Opportunity Party at 5% to 9.5% decides the coalition. Reduce kiwi positions before this.

catalysts.event: Japan: Q3 GDP
catalysts.note: The growth test behind the BoJ December case. The Bank raised its FY2026 growth forecast to 0.7% from 0.6% at the October meeting.

catalysts.event: United States: FOMC decision with new Economic Projections
catalysts.note: TradingEconomics forecasts 4.25%, which would be a second hike. The dot plot is the first full projection round since September and the last before Warsh reduces the number of voting meetings in 2027.

catalysts.event: Canada: BoC decision
catalysts.note: TradingEconomics forecasts 2.75%, making a second consecutive hike its base case and the main reason the Canadian dollar holds the top of this board.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: RBNZ decision with Monetary Policy Statement
catalysts.note: TradingEconomics forecasts 3.00%, the hike that was declined on October 28. By then the election result and the coalition will be known.

catalysts.event: Switzerland: SNB decision
catalysts.note: TradingEconomics forecasts 0.00%, unchanged. The SNB has been at zero since mid-2025 and is the only central bank on this board with no hike anywhere in its forecast path.

catalysts.event: Euro area: ECB decision with new staff projections
catalysts.note: Confirmed on the ECB calendar as the final 2026 meeting, with day one on December 16. Priced above 80% and one of Lagarde's last before she leaves on February 7. MUFG expects 25 basis points here and another in March.

catalysts.event: Japan: BoJ decision
catalysts.note: TradingEconomics forecasts 1.50%. Commerzbank calls it almost fully priced after the Bank declared underlying inflation had reached its 2% target.

catalysts.event: Strait of Hormuz, Iran-US talks and the AI capital-spending unwind
catalysts.note: Three undated risks that drive this whole board. Qatari mediators are in Tehran, Vice President Vance is seeking to reopen talks and Trump says the conflict will end very soon, while regional officials warn fighting could resume around the midterms. Separately, Apple and Nvidia results are the next tests of the AI capex story that took the Nasdaq down 5.3% in October.

geopolitics: The transmission chain from the Strait of Hormuz to this board got one link stronger over the weekend, and it is worth being precise about which link. On Friday Iran said four tankers struck mines in the Strait, explicitly disputing the US claim that the shipping lanes had been cleared; the Revolutionary Guard said a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels hit a naval mine and caught fire while on an unauthorised route, and described it as the third tanker to explode that day. UKMTO separately reported a small boat attaching two explosive devices to a tanker about 25 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman. Tehran continues to insist that vessels obtain permission before transiting. Then on Sunday, Reuters sources said OPEC+ agreed in principle at its November 1 meeting to leave December output targets unchanged, deferring the 2027 baselines to a fourth-quarter capacity review. Put those two together and the supply side of the oil market is being squeezed from both ends at once: no additional quota barrels, and a transit chokepoint that insurers must now price as mined. The group finished unwinding its 1.65 million barrel per day voluntary cut in September and most members are still producing well below target anyway, with exports running at 60-80% of normal in recent months, so the quota decision is less about volume than about signalling that the cartel will not lean against the war premium. WTI settled at 104.120 and plus 2.08%, Brent at 113.430 and plus 2.37%, with WTI plus 12.11% on the month and plus 81.33% on the year. The FX read runs in four directions. First, Canada: this is a direct terms-of-trade gain for a country that has just hiked for the first time in three years and whose central bank explicitly justified the move as reducing the risk that continuing high energy prices spread into other prices. That is why the Canadian dollar sits at the top of this board and why USD/CAD short stays the highest-conviction dollar trade here. Second, the hike cycle itself: the Bank of England named prolonged Middle East conflict and higher crude as the reason UK CPI is rising, the RBA named higher global energy prices following oil supply disruptions as a driver of its September hike, the ECB warned that elevated energy prices could fuel inflation while weighing on activity, and the SNB attributed the rise in Swiss inflation mainly to energy. Four of this board's eight central banks are tightening because of this one input, which means an accepted Iran deal would not weaken one currency - it would flatten four rate paths at once and is the single largest correlated risk in this file. Third, the equity and haven side, where the week produced a genuinely unusual result. Friday carried both an AI-driven equity crash and a fresh attack on shipping, and gold fell 3.62% to a one-year low rather than rallying, closing below Standard Chartered's 3,886 support, while the franc was flat. Only the yen behaved like a haven, rising against all seven other currencies here. That is the basis for this report cutting both gold and the franc and keeping the yen at plus 1 with a hawkish forward. Fourth, timing. The Wall Street Journal has reported that Washington warned Gulf states to prepare for a short, intense campaign against Iran, and regional officials and analysts now warn that fighting could resume around Tuesday's midterm vote - while simultaneously Vice President Vance is seeking to reopen talks, Qatari mediators are in Tehran carrying a revised US letter, and Trump says the conflict will end very soon. Both tails are live inside the same 72 hours. For a 4H book that means USOIL long and CAD long are correct but must be sized for a headline gap in either direction, and it means the Hormuz premium is the common factor sitting underneath USOIL, USD/CAD, CAD/CHF, AUD/CAD and the entire European rate complex - do not treat those as independent positions.
